blocks.html:
READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

The extinction of the cave bear

Hervé Bocherens, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Tübingen, Germany, says his colleagues find his research methods a little ‘crude'. He dissolves 30,000-year-old animal bones in hydrochloric acid, which is strong enough to burn through metal, soaks the bone solution in lye, cooks it at about 200 degrees Fahrenheit and freeze-dries it, until what's left is a speck of powder weighing less than one one-hundredth of an ounce. The method may be harsh, but the yield is precious – the biography of a cave bear as told through its chemical components. Bocherens is at the forefront of research on the bear, a European species that died out 25,000 years ago. People have been excavating cave bear remains for hundreds of years— in the Middle Ages, the massive skulls were attributed to dragons — but the past decade has seen a burst of discoveries about how the bears lived and why they became extinct. An abundance of bones has been found from Spain to Romania in caves where the animals once hibernated. ‘Caves are good places to preserve bones, and cave bears had the good sense to die there,' Bocherens says.

Along with mammoths, lions and woolly rhinos, cave bears (Ursus spelaeus) were once among Europe's most impressive creatures. Males weighed up to 1,500 pounds, 50 per cent more than the largest modern grizzly bears. Cave bears had wider heads than today's bears, and powerful shoulders and forelimbs. But the relationship between humans and cave bears has been mysterious. Were humans prey for the bears, or predators? Were bears the object of worship or fear?

Initially cave bears shared the continent of Europe, more than 100,000 years ago, with Neanderthals, a primitive species of humans. Modern humans arrived in Europe about 40,000 years ago, and were soon aware of the bears. They painted images of the animals on cave walls, and carved their likeness in fragments of mammoth tusk. The walls of France's Chauvet cave are painted with lions, hyenas and bears; dating back 32,000 years, these are perhaps the oldest paintings in the world. The painters weren't the cave's only occupants: the floor is covered with 150 cave bear skeletons, and its soft clay still holds paw prints. Most dramatically, a cave bear skull was perched on a stone slab in the center of one chamber, placed deliberately by some long-gone cave inhabitant. ‘There's no way to tell if it was just curiosity that made someone put a skull on the rock, or if it had religious significance,' says Bocherens.

Another discovery, hundreds of miles to the east of Chauvet, would shed light on the relationship between cave bears and humans. The Swabian Jura is a limestone plateau in southwestern Germany that is riddled with caves. A steel gate guards the Hohle Fels cave from vandals and curiosity-seekers. Floodlights in the cave's main chamber illuminate the ceiling, vaulted like a cathedral above 5,000 square feet of floor space. Long ago, as shown by the bones and tools that archaeologists have found, cave bears and human beings sought shelter here from winter weather.

In 2000, University of Tübingen paleobiologist Susanne Münzel unearthed a bear vertebra with a tiny triangular piece of flint embedded in it. The flint was likely a broken spear point, hard evidence of a successful bear hunt 29,000 years ago.

Münzel also found bear bones that had clearly been scraped by stone tools. Evidence for bears being a food source for early humans was shown by cut marks on skulls and leg bones where the flesh had been cut away. Many of the bones were from baby bears, perhaps caught while hibernating.

Cave bears disappeared not long after humans spread throughout Europe, and one theory is that hunting led to the bears' extinction. Hervé Bocherens' test tubes may hold the clues. Running his white powder through a mass spectrometer, he identifies different isotopes, or chemical forms, of elements such as carbon and nitrogen that reflect what the bears were eating and how quickly they grew. After studying hundreds of bones from dozens of sites in Europe, Bocherens has found that cave bears ate mainly plants.

This would have made bears particularly vulnerable to the last Ice Age, which began around 30,000 years ago. This Ice Age shortened or eliminated growing seasons, and altered the distributions of plant species across Europe. Cave bears began to move from their old territories, according to a DNA analysis of teeth found near the Danube River. The cave bear population there was relatively stable, with the same genetic patterns showing up generation after generation. But about 28,000 years ago, newcomers with different DNA patterns arrived — a possible sign of hungry bears suddenly on the move.

But changes in the climate can't be solely to blame for the bears' extinction. According to the latest study, by Erik Trinkaus and his colleagues at the Max Planck Institute, cave bear populations began a long, slow decline 50,000 years ago — well before the climate began to change. The new study supports a different explanation for the cave bears' demise. As Neanderthals, and then a growing population of modern humans moved into the caves of Europe, cave bears had fewer safe places to hibernate. An acute housing shortage may have been the final blow for these magnificent beasts.

Do the following statements agree with the information in Reading Passage 1?

In boxes 1–6 on your answer sheet, write:

  • TRUE if the statement agrees with the information

meta.matchedTitle: The extinction of the cave bear 洞熊的灭绝

passageNotes.label: 第一段
passageNotes.text: 德国图宾根大学的进化生物学家赫尔夫·博赫伦斯说，他的同事们觉得他的研究方法有点“粗糙”。他将3万年前的动物骨骼溶解在盐酸中，这种酸足以烧穿金属，然后将骨骼溶液浸泡在碱液中，在约200华氏度的温度下烹煮，并进行冷冻干燥，直到剩下不到百分之一盎司的粉末。这种方法可能很粗暴，但产出却很珍贵——通过其化学成分讲述的洞熊传记。博赫伦斯站在这种熊的研究前沿，这是一种2.5万年前灭绝的欧洲物种。人们挖掘洞熊遗骸已有数百年历史——在中世纪，巨大的头骨被认为是龙的——但在过去十年里，关于这些熊如何生活以及为何灭绝的发现层出不穷。从西班牙到罗马尼亚的洞穴中发现了大量骨骼，这些动物曾在那里冬眠。“洞穴是保存骨骼的好地方，洞熊有幸死在那里，”博赫伦斯说。

passageNotes.label: 第二段
passageNotes.text: 与猛犸象、狮子和毛犀一样，洞熊（Ursus spelaeus）曾是欧洲最令人印象深刻的生物之一。雄性体重可达1500磅，比现存最大的现代灰熊重50%。洞熊的头部比今天的熊更宽，肩膀和前肢强壮有力。但人类与洞熊之间的关系一直是个谜。人类是熊的猎物，还是捕食者？熊是崇拜的对象还是恐惧的源泉？

passageNotes.label: 第三段
passageNotes.text: 最初，洞熊与尼安德特人（一种原始人类）在十多万年前共同生活在欧洲大陆。现代人类约在4万年前到达欧洲，并很快意识到了这些熊的存在。他们在洞穴墙壁上绘制这些动物的图像，并在猛犸象牙的碎片上雕刻它们的肖像。法国肖维岩洞的墙壁上画有狮子、鬣狗和熊；这些画作可追溯到3.2万年前，可能是世界上最古老的绘画。这些画家并非洞穴唯一的居住者：地板上覆盖着150具洞熊骨架，其松软的粘土上仍保留着爪印。最引人注目的是，一个洞熊头骨被栖放在一个洞室中央的石板上，由某个早已逝去的洞穴居民有意放置。“无法判断是仅仅出于好奇心让某人把头骨放在岩石上，还是它具有宗教意义，”博赫伦斯说。

passageNotes.label: 第四段
passageNotes.text: 另一项发现，在肖维以东数百英里的地方，将揭示洞熊与人类之间的关系。施瓦本汝拉是德国西南部一个布满洞穴的石灰岩高原。一扇钢门守护着霍勒菲尔斯洞穴，防止破坏者和好奇者的进入。洞穴主室的聚光灯照亮了天花板，它像大教堂一样拱起在5000平方英尺的地面空间之上。很久以前，正如考古学家发现的骨骼和工具所示，洞熊和人类曾在这里躲避冬天的严寒。

passageNotes.label: 第五段
passageNotes.text: 2000年，图宾根大学的古生物学家苏珊娜·明策尔发掘出一块熊的椎骨，里面嵌着一小块三角形的燧石。这块燧石很可能是一支断裂的矛头，是2.9万年前一次成功猎熊的确凿证据。

passageNotes.label: 第六段
passageNotes.text: 明策尔还发现了明显被石器刮擦过的熊骨。熊骨上留下的切割痕迹，显示肉曾被从头骨和腿骨上割下，这证明了熊是早期人类的食物来源。许多骨头来自幼熊，可能是在它们冬眠时被捕获的。

passageNotes.label: 第七段
passageNotes.text: 洞熊在人类遍布欧洲后不久就消失了，一种理论认为捕猎导致了熊的灭绝。赫尔夫·博赫伦斯的试管可能持有线索。他将白色粉末通过质谱仪运行，识别出碳和氮等元素的不同同位素或化学形式，这些同位素反映了熊吃什么以及它们生长得多快。在研究了欧洲数十个地点的数百块骨骼后，博赫伦斯发现洞熊主要吃植物。

passageNotes.label: 第八段
passageNotes.text: 这将使熊在约3万年前开始的末次冰期中特别脆弱。这次冰期缩短或消除了生长季节，并改变了整个欧洲植物物种的分布。根据在多瑙河附近发现的牙齿的DNA分析，洞熊开始从它们的旧领地迁徙。那里的洞熊种群相对稳定，代代相传着相同的遗传模式。但大约2.8万年前，带有不同DNA模式的新来者抵达——这可能是饥饿的熊突然迁徙的迹象。

passageNotes.label: 第九段
passageNotes.text: 但气候变化不能完全归咎于熊的灭绝。根据马克斯·普朗克研究所的埃里克·特林考斯及其同事的最新研究，洞熊种群在5万年前就开始了漫长而缓慢的下降——远在气候开始变化之前。这项新研究支持了洞熊灭绝的另一种解释。随着尼安德特人，然后是日益增多的现代人类迁入欧洲的洞穴，洞熊冬眠的安全地方越来越少。严重的住房短缺可能已成为这些宏伟野兽的最后一击。

items.text:
(1) 题目 1：Bocherens' findings on cave bears involve measuring the length of complete bones. （博赫伦斯对洞熊的发现涉及测量完整骨骼的长度。）
答案：FALSE
解析：第一段描述他的方法是“dissolves... bones”（溶解骨骼）并分析其“chemical components”（化学成分），而非测量长度。

(2) 题目 2：Bocherens was the first person to conduct analytical research on cave bears in a laboratory. （博赫伦斯是第一个在实验室对洞熊进行分析研究的人。）
答案：NOT GIVEN
解析：第一段说他“is at the forefront of research”（处在研究前沿），但这不等于他是“the first person”（第一个人）。

(3) 题目 3：Cave bears have been extinct for 25,000 years. （洞熊已经灭绝了25,000年。）
答案：TRUE
解析：第一段明确指出洞熊是“a European species that died out 25,000 years ago”。

(4) 题目 4：At one time, people thought the excavated remains of bears were those of dragons. （曾几何时，人们认为挖掘出的熊的遗骸是龙的。）
答案：TRUE
解析：第一段提到在中世纪，“the massive skulls were attributed to dragons”。

(5) 题目 5：Modern grizzly bears are similar in size to cave bears. （现代灰熊与洞熊大小相似。）
答案：FALSE
解析：第二段说洞熊雄性比最大的现代灰熊“50 per cent more”（重50%），所以大小不相似。

(6) 题目 6：Neanderthals understood cave bear behaviour better than modern humans did. （尼安德特人比现代人更了解洞熊的行为。）
答案：NOT GIVEN
解析：文章描述了两者与洞熊的共存和互动，但并未对他们理解洞熊行为的深浅进行比较。

items.text:
(1) 题目 7：Over a hundred 7 \___\___ of cave bears, together with paw prints, were found on the floor of the cave. （超过一百具洞熊的7 \___\___和爪印在洞穴地面上被发现。）
答案：skeletons
解析：第三段说洞穴地面上覆盖着“150 cave bear skeletons”。

(2) 题目 8：The 8 \___\___ of a cave bear was found in a prominent position in the cave. （一个洞熊的8 \___\___被发现在洞穴一个显眼的位置。）
答案：skull
解析：第三段描述“a cave bear skull was perched on a stone slab in the center of one chamber”。

(3) 题目 9：Bones and tools found in the cave indicate it provided 9 \___\___ for both bears and humans. （洞穴中发现的骨骼和工具表明它为熊和人都提供了9 \___\___。）
答案：shelter
解析：第四段说洞熊和人类曾在此“sought shelter here from winter weather”。

(4) 题目 10：Isotopes from the bones indicate that 10 \___\___ were the cave bears' preferred food. （骨骼中的同位素表明10 \___\___是洞熊偏爱的食物。）
答案：plants
解析：第七段，博赫伦斯的研究发现“cave bears ate mainly plants”。

(5) 题目 11：The Ice Age changed vegetation growth in 11 \___\___ （冰河时代改变了11 \___\___的植被生长。）
答案：seasons
解析：第八段说冰期“shortened or eliminated growing seasons”。

(6) 题目 12：Support for the above explanation comes from a study of changes in the DNA in the 12 \___\___ of the population of cave bears near the Danube River at this time. （上述解释的支撑来自于一项对当时多瑙河附近洞熊种群12 \___\___中DNA变化的研究。）
答案：teeth
解析：第八段提到DNA分析是基于“teeth found near the Danube River”。

(7) 题目 13：Competition from Neanderthals and modern humans for caves may have reduced opportunities for cave bears to 13 \___\___. （与尼安德特人和现代人对洞穴的竞争可能减少了洞熊13 \___\___的机会。）
答案：hibernate
解析：第九段说洞熊“had fewer safe places to hibernate”。
